candidates.title: Hisense’s E7SF MiniLED TV Pairs Holiday Movies With 144Hz Gaming
candidates.full_text:
The holiday living room rarely sticks to one job. Hisense’s E7SF MiniLED TV is designed for that changing schedule, combining a 4K screen, native 144Hz refresh, and Fire TV for movies, sports, and games. With Black Friday putting home upgrades back on the agenda, its appeal lies in accommodating all that activity without turning every change of plans into another trip through the settings.

Of course, that starts with the room itself. A television has to share space with furniture, decorations, and people who didn’t come over to admire a spec sheet. The 65-inch model’s dual-position legs offer flexibility in how it sits on a cabinet. It’s a small physical detail, but one that acknowledges your living room probably wasn’t designed around the television’s feet.

Once everyone settles in, the next challenge is agreeing on something to watch. Fire TV brings streaming apps into the television, while the Alexa-enabled voice remote lets you search without pecking out a title letter by letter. It won’t settle the debate over another holiday comedy, though. At least finding the candidates doesn’t have to become the evening’s main entertainment.

An afternoon gathering also means daylight, lamps, and a screen that’s rarely the only thing drawing attention. The E7SF’s AI Light Sensor adjusts backlight output to suit ambient lighting, while AI Picture handles scene-based brightness, contrast, and color adjustments. Those are different jobs, both aimed at reducing manual tweaking. There’s enough to organize during the holidays without adding picture settings to the list.

Then football comes on, and suddenly everyone has an opinion about what just happened. Hisense’s AI Sports Mode adjusts picture and sound settings for sports, while motion processing is designed to make fast action easier to follow. It gives a fast-moving broadcast its own treatment, rather than assuming the same processing suits a slow conversation in a movie and a receiver sprinting toward the end zone.

When a controller replaces the broadcast, the native 144Hz panel takes on a different role. With compatible hardware and games, it can display high-frame-rate action, while variable refresh rate and AMD FreeSync Premium help synchronize the screen with the source to reduce tearing. That matters when you’re steering through a corner, even if it can’t explain why your cousin keeps beating you.

By evening, the lights can come down and the movie can finally start. Here, MiniLED backlighting divides illumination into independently controlled zones, allowing brighter and darker areas to be treated differently within the same frame. Hi-QLED adds quantum dots for a broader palette of colors. A film’s glowing decorations and shadowy streets give those systems different jobs within the same scene.

There’s also a welcome acknowledgment that movies don’t always need more processing. Filmmaker Mode switches off motion smoothing and other enhancements while preserving the source’s frame rate and aspect ratio. Alongside support for Dolby Vision and HDR10+, it gives movie night both broad HDR compatibility and a way to retain cinematic motion. A familiar holiday favorite doesn’t need to move like an afternoon soap opera.

Sound deserves a place in that evening, too, and the E7SF includes Dolby Atmos support. The 65-inch model uses a 2.0-channel speaker system, keeping basic listening self-contained, with eARC for anyone who wants to connect an external sound system. That leaves room to build around the television later without making a collection of separate speakers the starting point for an evening together.

Eventually, the guests head home, the decorations come down, and the living room returns to its less festive schedule. That’s when the same screen has to accommodate a quiet episode after work or a game before bed. The E7SF’s mix of automatic adjustments and content-specific options makes sense in that setting, where the evening’s biggest ambition might simply be getting comfortable and leaving the remote alone.

candidates.title: LEGO’s McLaren W1 Speed Champions set is the shelf build for F1 fans who want one car
candidates.full_text:
Some LEGO cars are fun because they start a collection. The McLaren W1 Speed Champions set is better if you only want one small build that looks fast enough to earn its spot on a shelf.

Price: $22.49 (From $27.99) Where to Buy: Amazon

LEGO’s official 2026 Speed Champions page lists the McLaren W1 as part of the current lineup. The pitch is clear: this is a road legal McLaren turned into a compact display build for ages 9 and up, not a huge weekend project.

It’s based on the fastest accelerating road legal McLaren, with details like an adjustable rear wing, cockpit, and air intake ducts on the sides and hood.

That’s a lot of supercar energy for something that doesn’t need a whole desk.

The McLaren W1 isn’t the only 2026 Speed Champions car with a big name. LEGO’s current list includes Ferrari, Bugatti, Mercedes AMG F1, Audi F1, movie cars, and a full mix of race and road machines.

That crowded lineup is exactly why the W1 stands out.

It has the McLaren name and a modern hypercar shape. It has enough real car detail to feel more grown up than a random toy car. It still sits in the small Speed Champions format.

If you like cars, F1, or McLaren enough to want something physical on your shelf, this is the kind of set that makes sense without turning into a giant build project.

LEGO calls out the adjustable rear wing, cockpit, and air intakes on the hood and sides. Those are the features that matter because Speed Champions sets live or die by whether the tiny version still reads like the real car.

The W1 has a cleaner pitch than some collector sets.

It doesn’t need a light kit, a giant footprint, or a complicated display case. Build it once, place it somewhere you’ll actually see it, and let the shape do the work.

It also fits a simple test: fun first, but not useless. This is a small desk or shelf object that happens to have real car nerd appeal.

The tempting comparison isn’t another McLaren LEGO set. The better question is whether you want a single display car or a bigger LEGO habit.

LEGO’s 2026 Speed Champions page is packed with options, and that can get dangerous fast.

The McLaren W1 is for the person who wants the sleek supercar lane. It’s less about team colors and more about the shape.

Racing fandom can get expensive fast, from apparel to full memorabilia hauls. A small LEGO build hits the same collector itch from a calmer angle: sometimes the fun thing is the small object you’ll actually keep around. A small LEGO build is a more controlled way to put that interest on your desk.

Buy the McLaren W1 if you want a compact LEGO car that feels current, clean, and display ready. It’s an especially easy gift for someone who likes McLaren but doesn’t need a giant Technic build.

Skip it if you want minifig heavy play value, a full F1 team car, or the most nostalgia loaded Speed Champions set. This is a sleek shelf car, not a whole racing universe.

Price: $22.49 (From $27.99) Where to Buy: Amazon

That focus is the whole point. Buy this one if that sounds right.

candidates.title: A Spider-Inspired Stool With a Hidden Grip in Its Eyes
candidates.full_text:
A thumb in a spider’s eye sounds like a terrible idea. On Fabrício Auler’s Tocaia Stool, it’s how you’re supposed to pick the thing up. Four dimples sit near the rim of the round wooden seat, two large ones flanked by two smaller ones. At first they look like a face. Then you see the photo of a hand grabbing the stool, and you realize the face is also the handle.

A little stool is useful partly because it can go wherever you need it, from the entryway when you’re putting on shoes to the living room when you need another seat. But a round seat gives you nowhere obvious to grab. Auler’s concept, which he built as a prototype, borrows the face of a jumping spider to give your thumb a place to settle while your fingers curl under the rim. It’s a small fix for a piece of furniture you’re likely to move more often than you sit on it.

The close-up of the grip explains why those dimples sit so close to the edge. Your hand can pinch the seat without reaching across it, and none of the recesses goes all the way through. A cutout would be easier to spot and might give you more to hold on to, but it would also make the handle the first thing you noticed. Here, most of the seat stays flat, so if the stool ends up next to the couch with a book on it, the spider gets to keep its face.

I like that Auler stopped at four legs. The project sketch puts a picture of a jumping spider next to an ordinary round stool, and the finished shape lands closer to the stool than you might expect. The legs angle outward, but they don’t bend into anything resembling a spider’s joints. The face does most of the work. Had Auler gone for eight legs, I’d probably read the whole thing as a prop. With four, it looks like furniture right up until it looks back at you.

The finishes shift that balance more than I expected. The pale wood version looks almost anonymous from the side. On the black one, light catches the inside of each dimple and makes the eyes much harder to miss. My favorite is the version with a warm wood seat and legs that darken toward the floor. It has enough of the black stool’s creepiness to carry the joke, but the grain across the top still makes it look at home next to a stack of paperbacks.

Tocaia means “ambush” in Brazilian Portuguese, which fits Auler’s description of a stool lying in wait between the bed and the bathroom. The project photos take that idea about as far as it can go: one shows the black stool dangling on a white thread above someone’s head. I prefer the shot where it’s under a cream sweater, with just enough of the seat showing for the eyes to peek out. A stool disappearing under yesterday’s clothes requires considerably less imagination than one descending from the ceiling.

The workshop shots bring it back down to earth. They show a round seat blank, legs laid out on the bench, and the recesses already cut into the bare wood. I appreciate seeing those holes before the black finish turns them into eyes. They make it clear how little Auler had to change about a familiar object to give it a personality. Even if you never see a spider, the larger dimples still tell you where to put your thumb.

That’s why I’d rather have the Tocaia by the front door than on a shelf as a conversation piece. The joke has a better chance of landing when someone actually reaches for the stool and discovers what the eyes are for. I’d still park it well clear of the route to the bathroom, though. A stool that looks like it’s waiting to trip you is funnier when it doesn’t get the chance.
